name: Big Two
description: Big Two (also known as Choh Dai Di or Pusoy Dos) is the quintessential Chinese climbing card game. It features a unique ranking hierarchy where the 2 is the most powerful card and the 3 is the weakest. Players compete to empty their hands by playing increasingly higher combinations of cards, including singles, pairs, and standard five-card poker hands. The game is highly strategic, requiring players to manage their high cards (deuces) while clearing their weaker low cards through tactical passing and control of the lead.

history.origins: Emerging in coastal China (likely Shanghai or Hong Kong) in the mid-20th century, Big Two combined the climbing mechanics of traditional Chinese games with the globally recognized ranking of poker hands.
timeline: 1980s: Rapidly spreads through Hong Kong and Taiwan as a favorite social game.
1990s: Introduced to Southeast Asia, becoming 'Pusoy Dos' in the Philippines.
2000s: Digital adaptations on mobile and web platforms bring the game to a global audience.
Present: Remains one of the most widely played card games in East Asia.
history.cultural: A staple of social gatherings and university life in Chinese communities. It is often played for small stakes based on the number of cards remaining in losers' hands.
history.evolution: Regional variations in suit hierarchy (e.g., whether Spades or Diamonds is the highest suit) created distinct styles of play in Hong Kong vs. Taiwan.

setup.dealing: Deal the entire deck clockwise (13 cards to each player). The player holding the 3 of Diamonds leads the first trick.

rules.objective: Be the first player to shed all cards from your hand.
rules.gameplay: 1. **The Lead**: Player with 3♦ must play it (as a single or in a combo). 2. **Climbing**: Each player in turn must play a combination of the same type (single, pair, triple, or 5-card hand) that is higher in rank than the previous play. 3. **Ranks**: 2 (High) > A > K > Q ... > 3 (Low). 4. **Suits**: Spades > Hearts > Clubs > Diamonds (used to break ties in same-rank plays). 5. **Passing**: A player can pass at any time. When 3 players pass, the last player to play starts a new trick with any combo.
keyRules: 5-card combinations must follow poker rankings: Royal Flush > Straight Flush > 4-of-a-Kind > Full House > Flush > Straight.
The rank of a 5-card combo is determined by its highest card (e.g., an Ace-high Flush beats a King-high Flush).
If you pass, you can still play later in the same trick cycle if the lead has not been reset.

strategy.basic: Get rid of your lowest cards (3s, 4s, 5s) early by leading them when you have control. Save your 2s to regain the lead when opponents play their high cards.
strategy.intermediate: Combination Management: If you have a single 2 and a pair of 2s, don't waste the pair on a single lead. Wait for someone to play a high pair to trap them.
strategy.advanced: Card Counting: There are only four 2s and four Aces. Once they are played, the Kings become the most powerful cards. Track them to know when your 'medium' cards are guaranteed to win the lead.
tips: Avoid being left with only one card that is difficult to play (like a single 3).
Use your 5-card hands to shed a large volume of low cards at once.

variations.name: Pusoy Dos (Philippines)
variations.description: Standard rules but often uses a different suit hierarchy (Diamonds high).

variations.name: Taiwanese Big Two
variations.description: Allows 'Dragon' sequences (13 cards) and has different multipliers for 2s left in hand.
variations.emptyOverridesReason: Taiwanese Big Two adjusts dragon sequences and scoring multipliers; this profile documents it textually until dedicated engine overrides are introduced.

scoring.description: Losers receive penalty points based on remaining cards (1x, 2x, or 3x multipliers).
scoring.winCondition: First player to empty their hand wins the round.

synthesis.shortDescription: Master the world's most popular climbing game. Manage your powerful deuces, build tactical sequences, and outmaneuver your opponents to empty your hand first. From social gatherings to high-stakes matches, Big Two is the gold standard of East Asian card gaming.
